mc.q: Which range category does Bluetooth typically fall under?
mc.explain: Bluetooth is a short-range (~10 m) Wireless Personal Area Network technology.

mc.q: Streaming Netflix on home Wi-Fi is an example of:
mc.explain: Home Wi-Fi (802.11) is a Wireless Local Area Network.

mc.q: Smartwatch step tracking (syncing to a phone) uses which technology?
mc.explain: Wearables sync to phones over Bluetooth (usually BLE).

mc.q: The main benefit of WWAN during a disaster is:
mc.explain: Wide-area cellular/satellite coverage keeps working when local infrastructure is down.

mc.q: Which IEEE standard is used for Wi-Fi 6?
mc.explain: 802.11ax = Wi-Fi 6. 802.11ac = Wi-Fi 5, 802.15.4 = ZigBee PHY/MAC, 802.3 = Ethernet.

mc.q: A Wi-Fi access point sending beacons every 100 ms is operating at which OSI layer?
mc.explain: Beacons are 802.11 MAC management frames: Layer 2 (Data Link).

mc.q: Which frame type does a ZigBee device send when it wants to find a network?
mc.explain: In 802.15.4/ZigBee, a device scans by sending a Beacon Request; coordinators/routers reply with beacons. (Probe request is the Wi-Fi equivalent.)

mc.q: Why do IoT devices often use 2.4 GHz instead of 5 GHz?
mc.explain: Lower frequency has less free-space loss and penetrates walls better. 2.4 GHz is actually MORE crowded.

mc.q: Which statement about packet switching vs circuit switching is true?
options: Circuit switching idle times waste capacity
Packet switching cannot handle bursty traffic
mc.explain: A circuit's capacity is dedicated even when nothing is sent, so idle periods waste it. Packet switching shares bandwidth dynamically and suits bursty traffic.

mc.q: Which wireless tech uses frequency hopping as part of its standard?
mc.explain: Bluetooth uses FHSS: 79 x 1 MHz channels, 1600 hops/s (adaptive hopping avoids busy channels).

mc.q: A device roaming between APs of the same SSID sends what?
mc.explain: Reassociation Request = moving to a new AP within the same ESS.

mc.q: In WPA2, which exchange provides the cryptographic material for the session key?
mc.explain: The 4-way handshake exchanges ANonce/SNonce so both sides derive the PTK from the PMK.

mc.q: What does IMSI stand for in GSM?
mc.explain: IMSI: the permanent subscriber identity stored on the SIM.

mc.q: Which GSM component stores subscriber location and status (for subscribers currently in its area)?
mc.explain: The VLR holds temporary location/status data for subscribers in its area. The HLR is the permanent home database (not an option here).

mc.q: SIM cards improve security primarily by:
mc.explain: The SIM holds the secret key Ki and runs A3/A8; Ki never leaves the card.

mc.q: Why does GSM use a Temporary Mobile Subscriber Identity (TMSI)?
options: To hide IMSI over the air
mc.explain: TMSI provides identity confidentiality so the IMSI isn't broadcast and trackable.

mc.q: Which multiple access technique does GSM primarily use on the air interface?
mc.explain: GSM: FDMA into 200 kHz carriers, each TDMA-split into 8 time slots.

mc.q: In a distributed system, which property hides the location of resources?
mc.explain: Transparency (location transparency) hides where resources physically reside.

mc.q: Which is NOT a characteristic of a distributed system?
options: Single point of failure by design
mc.explain: Distributed systems aim to avoid single points of failure.

mc.q: Leader election algorithms in distributed systems are primarily used to:
mc.explain: Leader election picks one coordinator node (e.g., Bully, Ring algorithms).

mc.q: Which protocol secures Diameter signaling in LTE/5G core networks?
mc.explain: 3GPP Network Domain Security (NDS/IP) protects inter-operator Diameter with IPsec.

mc.q: Which technology makes blockchain records tamper-resistant?
mc.explain: Each block contains the hash of the previous block; altering one block breaks every later link.

mc.q: Which data/signal combination describes a traditional landline telephone call?
mc.explain: Voice (analog data) carried as a continuous electrical waveform (analog signal).

mc.q: For transmitting login credentials, which is more secure: analog or digital transmission?
options: Analog, because continuous waveforms are harder to copy
Digital, because it supports CRC, parity, encryption, and message authentication
Analog, because it needs no repeaters
They are equally secure; only the medium matters
mc.explain: Digital allows CRC/parity, encryption, and message authentication. Analog lacks structure and can't detect tampering.

mc.q: In a very noisy environment, which is the safer way to raise data rate: add bandwidth or add signal levels (M)?
options: Add more signal levels; it needs no extra spectrum
Add bandwidth; more levels are harder to tell apart in noise, causing bit errors
Either one; noise does not affect signal levels
Add more levels, because errors help mask the signal from attackers
mc.explain: More levels are closer together, so noise causes bit errors, which can break TLS handshakes and key exchanges.

mc.q: Which switching approach reserves a dedicated end-to-end path before data flows, fitting constant-rate voice calls?
mc.explain: Circuit switching sets up a dedicated path with fixed bandwidth. Packet switching suits bursty data.

mc.q: In the packet-size / MTU ping lab, why isn't it always better to send fewer, larger packets?
options: Larger packets are always dropped by firewalls
A packet above the path MTU must be fragmented (or fails with 'don't fragment'), adding overhead and risk
Smaller packets are illegal on the Internet
mc.explain: Fragmentation adds headers and reassembly work; losing one fragment loses the whole packet.

mc.q: On the 2.4 GHz band, which channels are non-overlapping?
mc.explain: Channels 1, 6, 11. If congested on 6, move to 1 or 11.

mc.q: Why can a single SSID show up with multiple BSSIDs?
options: Multiple APs extend coverage and allow roaming / load balancing
Each BSSID is a different password
The SSID is being spoofed every time
mc.explain: One SSID across several APs (each with its own BSSID/MAC) extends coverage and enables roaming.

mc.q: AP-A: 80% signal on 5 GHz, low congestion. AP-B: 55% signal on 2.4 GHz, many neighbors. Which gives higher capacity?
options: AP-A, because higher signal (better SNR) and wider, less-crowded 5 GHz spectrum
Neither; capacity depends only on the password
AP-B, because more neighbors means more shared bandwidth
mc.explain: Shannon: capacity grows with bandwidth and SNR. AP-A wins on both.

mc.q: A WPA2 handshake-capture-and-crack attack works because the captured file contains which messages?
options: The plaintext password in the beacon
The EAPOL messages of the 4-way handshake
The DNS queries of every client
mc.explain: EAPOL messages let an attacker test passphrases offline (e.g., RockYou wordlist).

mc.q: Deauth and evil-twin attacks are possible because which 802.11 frames are unprotected?
options: Management frames (beacons, deauth, association), sent in cleartext even on WPA2/WPA3
mc.explain: Cleartext management frames can be forged (deauth) or spoofed (fake beacons). 802.11w/PMF mitigates this.

mc.q: A PC is paired with both a phone and a headset at once. In piconet terms, the PC is:
mc.explain: One master coordinates up to 7 active slaves and sets the hopping sequence/clock.

mc.q: In the Wireshark VPN lab, what changed between the no-VPN capture and the VPN capture?
options: Packets were still visible, but their contents became unreadable ciphertext
The Wi-Fi password appeared in plaintext
mc.explain: Without VPN: plaintext DNS/HTTP. With VPN: you see packets exist, not what they contain.

mc.q: Which attack would a VPN NOT fully protect you against?
options: A deauthentication attack, because it targets unprotected 802.11 management frames
mc.explain: Deauth forges management frames below the tunnel and knocks you off regardless of the VPN.

mc.q: Which Wi-Fi configuration is safer for confidentiality?
options: An Open network, because anyone can connect
mc.explain: Open encrypts nothing. Hidden SSIDs and MAC filtering are trivially bypassed and encrypt nothing.

mc.q: A channel spans 3 MHz to 4 MHz with SNR = 24 dB (~251). Approximate Shannon capacity?
mc.explain: B = 1 MHz. C = B log2(1+SNR) = 10^6 x log2(252) ~ 8 Mbps.

mc.q: For C = 8 Mbps and B = 1 MHz, how many signal levels M does Nyquist require?
mc.explain: C = 2B log2 M -> 8 = 2 log2 M -> M = 16.

mc.q: Why do digital systems use repeaters rather than amplifiers?
options: Repeaters regenerate a clean signal; amplifiers boost the noise too
mc.explain: A repeater recovers the 1s/0s and retransmits cleanly, so noise doesn't accumulate.

mc.q: A gain of +3 dB corresponds to roughly:
If coherence bandwidth Bc >> signal bandwidth Bs, the channel experiences:
mc.explain: The whole signal sees the same channel response: flat fading. Fast vs slow fading depends on coherence time.

mc.q: Free-space path loss increases with:
mc.explain: FSPL ~ (4 pi d f / c)^2, which is why 2.4 GHz reaches farther than 5 GHz.

mc.q: Which packet-switching approach establishes a preplanned route and delivers packets in order?
mc.explain: Virtual circuit: route set up first, but packets are still buffered/queued (not a dedicated path).

mc.q: In TCP/IP encapsulation, what does the IP layer produce?
mc.explain: Data -> TCP segment -> IP datagram -> network-access frame.

mc.q: Why does 802.11 use CSMA/CA instead of CSMA/CD?
options: Wireless radios can't reliably detect collisions while transmitting (e.g., hidden terminals)
mc.explain: A radio can't listen while sending, and hidden nodes can't hear each other, so 802.11 avoids collisions instead of detecting them.

mc.q: Which mechanism addresses the hidden-terminal problem in 802.11?
mc.explain: The AP's CTS is heard by all stations, including the hidden one, which then defers.

mc.q: An Extended Service Set (ESS) is:
options: A single AP and its clients
Two or more BSSs connected by a distribution system
mc.explain: BSS = one AP + stations. ESS = multiple BSSs joined by a DS, appearing as one network (one SSID).

mc.q: RTS, CTS, and ACK are which type of 802.11 frame?
mc.explain: Control frames manage medium access. Beacons/association/deauth are management frames.

mc.q: In WPA2, the PTK is derived from:
options: PMK, ANonce, SNonce, and both MAC addresses
mc.explain: PTK = PRF(PMK, ANonce, SNonce, AP MAC, STA MAC). The GTK protects broadcast/multicast.

mc.q: KRACK exploits which weakness?
options: Replaying handshake message 3 forces key reinstallation and nonce reuse
mc.explain: Reinstalling an in-use key resets nonces, so keystream is reused and traffic can be decrypted/replayed.

mc.q: WPA3-Personal resists offline dictionary attacks by replacing PSK with:
mc.explain: SAE: each password guess requires a live interaction, so captured handshakes can't be cracked offline.

mc.q: A device participating in two or more piconets forms a:
mc.explain: Overlapping piconets linked by a shared device = scatternet.

mc.q: ZigBee is built on which IEEE standard?
mc.explain: 802.15.4 defines PHY/MAC. 802.15.1 is (classic) Bluetooth.

mc.q: Which ZigBee device type starts the network and is always present?
mc.explain: One coordinator per network; routers extend the mesh; end devices sleep to save power.

mc.q: A major GSM weakness enabling fake base stations (IMSI catchers) is:
options: Only the phone is authenticated; the network is not
mc.explain: GSM authentication is one-way, so a rogue BTS can impersonate the network (and even request no encryption). 3G/UMTS added mutual auth.

mc.q: Which GSM algorithm generates the session cipher key Kc?
mc.explain: A3 = authentication (SRES), A8 = key generation (Kc), A5 = air-interface encryption.

mc.q: Where is the subscriber secret key Ki stored?
options: On the SIM and in the AuC
mc.explain: Ki is shared only between the SIM and the Authentication Center.

mc.q: In Bitcoin, double spending is prevented by:
options: A timestamped, proof-of-work chain; the longest chain is accepted
mc.explain: Nodes accept the chain with the most cumulative work; rewriting history requires out-computing the honest majority.

mc.q: An attacker can rewrite Bitcoin history only if they control:
options: A majority of the network's hash power
mc.explain: The 51% attack: with majority CPU power, an attacker can outpace honest nodes.

terms.back: BSS: one AP + its stations. ESS: multiple BSSs joined by a distribution system, shared SSID.
PMK: from passphrase (PSK) or 802.1X. PTK: per-session unicast key from 4-way handshake. GTK: group key for broadcast/multicast.
Probe request: client actively asks for networks. Beacon: AP passively advertises itself (~every 100 ms).
Two stations can hear the AP but not each other, so they collide at the AP. Fixed by RTS/CTS.
C = B log2(1 + SNR). Max error-free rate for bandwidth B and SNR (linear, not dB).
C = 2B log2 M. Noise-free; M = number of signal levels.
Maximum Transmission Unit: largest packet a link carries without fragmentation (1500 bytes on Ethernet).
Quality of Service: prioritizes latency-sensitive traffic (VoIP, video calls) when links are congested.
IMSI: permanent identity on SIM. TMSI: temporary alias sent over the air to hide the IMSI.
Network sends RAND; SIM computes SRES = A3(Ki, RAND) and Kc = A8(Ki, RAND); network compares SRES; A5 encrypts with Kc.
Fake base station exploiting GSM's one-way authentication to capture IMSIs or downgrade encryption.
2.4 GHz ISM, 79 x 1 MHz channels, FHSS at 1600 hops/s, IEEE 802.15.1, piconet = 1 master + 7 active slaves.
IEEE 802.15.4, low power/low rate, mesh. Coordinator, router, end device. Joins via beacon request.
Key Reinstallation Attack: replay message 3 of the 4-way handshake, forcing nonce reuse so traffic can be decrypted.
Protected Management Frames: authenticates deauth/disassoc frames to stop forged deauth attacks. Required in WPA3.
Resource sharing, concurrency, transparency, scalability, fault tolerance, openness. No single point of failure by design.
